sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's idioms for design patterns diverge significantly from the Gang of Four catalogue used in Java and C++. Go favours composition over inheritance, interfaces over abstract classes, and first-class functions over visitor hierarchies. Interviewers probe this module to see whether you apply Go-idiomatic patterns rather than porting Java patterns into Go. The functional options pattern, middleware chaining, and sync.Once singleton are the three patterns most frequently cited in Go interviews and code reviews. Being able to explain why Go achieves these patterns with fewer lines and fewer abstractions than Java counterparts is a strong differentiator.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Go patterns leverage the language's first-class functions, interfaces, and the sync package. Functional options: a constructor accepts variadic func(*Config) arguments; each option mutates the config struct; the constructor reads the final config after applying all options. Middleware chain: each middleware is a func(http.Handler) http.Handler; composing them with a loop or a library like alice builds a layered call stack. Repository pattern: define an interface (UserRepository) and a concrete implementation (PostgresUserRepository); handlers depend on the interface, not the implementation — testable via mock. Singleton with sync.Once: the instance is created exactly once regardless of how many goroutines race to initialise it; zero-value sync.Once is ready to use. Observer with channels: event publishers send to a channel; subscriber goroutines receive; channels provide natural back-pressure.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Functional options — type Option func(*Server); NewServer(opts ...Option) applies each; clean API, zero value defaults, backward compatible. 2. Options vs Builder — Options avoid a mutable builder object and are safe to call in any order; Builder is more natural when construction order matters or validation must happen per-step. 3. Middleware chain — func(http.Handler) http.Handler; compose with a loop from outermost to innermost; execution order matches wrap order. 4. Repository pattern — depend on interfaces; swap implementations for tests; the interface lives in the domain package, not the infrastructure package (dependency inversion). 5. Dependency injection — pass dependencies as constructor arguments; avoid global singletons; wire (Google) or fx (Uber) can generate the wiring from providers. 6. Observer with channels — publisher holds a slice of chan Event; broadcasts by sending to each; consider closing channels to signal shutdown. 7. sync.Once singleton — once.Do(func(){ instance = &T{} }); thread-safe, no locks needed in the calling code. 8. Avoid over-engineering — Go favours simple flat code; introduce patterns only when they reduce duplication or improve testability.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: Explain the functional options pattern and why it is preferred over a config struct argument. — A plain config struct requires callers to set every field or accept the zero value; options allow per-field defaults without requiring callers to know the full struct shape, and adding a new option is backward compatible. Q: How is the middleware chain pattern implemented in Go? — A middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler; you compose them by calling each wrapper with the next handler as argument; the result is a chain where each layer can execute code before and after calling the next. Q: Why use sync.Once for a singleton instead of a package-level init()? — init() runs at package load time even if the singleton is never used (wasted resources, slow startup); Once defers creation until first use and is still thread-safe. Q: Where should a repository interface be defined — in the domain package or the infrastructure package? — Domain package; the domain code defines what it needs (an abstraction), and the infrastructure package provides the implementation. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle. Q: How does observer with channels differ from traditional observer with callbacks? — Channels provide built-in back-pressure (a full channel blocks the sender) and work naturally with Go's concurrency model; callbacks require manual synchronisation if called from multiple goroutines.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "My default Go API for any struct with more than a couple of required parameters is the functional options pattern — I define an options struct with sensible zero-value defaults, expose exported option functions, and accept them as variadic arguments in the constructor. It keeps the constructor signature stable as the config grows, and callers only specify the options they actually care about. For structuring application layers I use the repository pattern: handlers or use-case functions depend on an interface defined in the domain package, and the PostgreSQL or Redis implementation lives in an infrastructure package. That boundary makes unit-testing trivial — I just pass a mock that implements the interface. For singletons like a database pool or a metrics client, I use sync.Once rather than init(), so the cost is only paid if the component is actually used. I avoid the classic Gang of Four patterns like Decorator or Visitor unless Go's composition and interface embedding genuinely aren't enough — which is rare."
